title: The History of Timekeeping
context: A university lecture on how humans have measured time, from ancient devices to atomic clocks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture continues our series on the history of technology, and we're going to look at something we all take for granted: the measurement of time. What I want to show you is that every leap forward in timekeeping was driven not by curiosity alone, but by very practical social and economic pressures.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: I'll move roughly in chronological order, though it's worth flagging now that the jumps between periods are not smooth. Timekeeping technology can sit still for centuries and then change twice within fifty years, usually for reasons that have nothing to do with clockmaking itself.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's begin in ancient Egypt, around three and a half thousand years ago. The earliest instruments we have evidence for were remarkably simple. A vertical post or obelisk was placed in an open courtyard, and priests tracked the position of its shadow as the sun moved across the sky. In other words, the whole system depended on sunlight, which of course made it useless at night or in overcast weather.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: That limitation prompted the next major invention. To measure the hours of darkness, the Egyptians, and later the Greeks, developed what we call the water clock. A vessel was filled and allowed to drain through a small opening at a supposedly steady rate, with markings on the inside indicating how much time had passed.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Now, these devices were certainly an improvement, but they had a serious weakness that's often overlooked. The rate at which liquid flows through a narrow opening changes with temperature. On a cold morning the flow slowed dramatically, so a winter hour and a summer hour were simply not the same length. Precision, in the modern sense, was still a long way off.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's now jump forward to medieval Europe, because this is where mechanical timekeeping really begins. Interestingly, the first true mechanical clocks were not built for merchants or governments. They appeared in monasteries, where the daily routine of communal prayer had to happen at fixed hours, even in the middle of the night. Religious discipline, not commerce, was the original driver.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The technical breakthrough at the heart of these machines was a mechanism called the escapement. This is a device that interrupts the fall of a weight, releasing its energy in small, regular bursts rather than all at once. It's the escapement that produces the familiar ticking sound, and virtually every mechanical clock since has depended on some version of it.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Even so, early tower clocks could gain or lose fifteen minutes a day. The real transformation in accuracy came in the seventeenth century, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens applied the regular swing of a pendulum to clockwork. Almost overnight, the daily error dropped from minutes to seconds. It's hard to overstate what a revolution that was.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: What's particularly interesting is what happened next at sea. In the eighteenth century, sailors could calculate their latitude from the sun, but establishing longitude required knowing the exact time back at their home port, and pendulum clocks were hopeless on a rolling ship. The British government offered an enormous prize for a solution, and it was eventually claimed by a self-taught carpenter, John Harrison, whose marine chronometer kept accurate time even in violent seas.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Now let's turn to the nineteenth century, when the pressure on timekeeping shifted from navigation to coordination. For most of history, every town had kept its own local time, set by the sun overhead, and nobody minded that noon in one city came minutes after noon in another. It was the expansion of the railways that made this intolerable, because publishing a workable timetable across hundreds of stations demanded a single standard time.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The twentieth century then brought two further leaps. In the nineteen twenties, engineers discovered that a small piece of quartz vibrates at an extremely stable frequency when electricity is applied, and this discovery eventually made cheap, accurate watches available to almost everyone.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Quartz technology, incidentally, never really left us. It's what sits inside the watch on most people's wrist today, humming away at a frequency tuned specifically so that dividing it down gives a clean one-second pulse.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: And then, in the nineteen fifties, came the most precise instruments ever constructed. Modern atomic clocks work by counting the natural oscillations of caesium atoms, which vibrate over nine billion times a second. A clock of this kind would drift by less than one second over a hundred million years, and it is this standard that now defines the length of a second itself.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: You might reasonably ask why anyone needs such extraordinary precision. The answer is sitting in your pocket. Satellite navigation works by comparing time signals from orbiting satellites, and because those signals travel at the speed of light, an error of a millionth of a second would put your position out by hundreds of metres. Without atomic timekeeping, there is simply no GPS.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: None of this, incidentally, means the story stops with the caesium clocks I've just described. Optical clocks now in development promise to be roughly a hundred times more stable again, for reasons that have nothing to do with GPS and everything to do with detecting the tiny gravitational effects predicted by general relativity. But that's a lecture for another year.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: So, to sum up, the story of timekeeping is really a story about society's changing demands: religious routine, ocean navigation, railway coordination, and now global positioning. Each generation needed a finer slice of time than the last, and each invention reshaped daily life in ways its makers never anticipated. Next week, we'll look at how calendars, rather than clocks, came to be standardised. Thank you.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.sentence: Egyptian priests told the time by following the movement of a tall post's ___.
questions.explanation: "Priests tracked the position of its shadow as the sun moved across the sky." The one-word limit rules out "the sun's position".

questions.sentence: To keep track of time during the hours of darkness, the Egyptians and Greeks invented the ___.
questions.explanation: "The Egyptians, and later the Greeks, developed what we call the water clock." Two words are allowed, and "water" alone would not name the device.

questions.sentence: These draining vessels were unreliable because changes in ___ altered how quickly the liquid escaped.
questions.explanation: "The rate at which liquid flows through a narrow opening changes with temperature." The lecturer then gives the cold-morning example to reinforce it.

questions.sentence: The earliest mechanical clocks were installed in ___ to signal fixed hours of prayer.
questions.explanation: "They appeared in monasteries, where the daily routine of communal prayer had to happen at fixed hours." Note the lecturer explicitly rules out merchants and governments first.

questions.sentence: A component known as the ___ releases a falling weight's energy in small, even bursts.
questions.explanation: "A mechanism called the escapement." The phrase "called the" is a reliable signal that a term you need is coming.

questions.sentence: Huygens dramatically improved accuracy by regulating clockwork with a swinging ___.
questions.explanation: Huygens "applied the regular swing of a pendulum to clockwork". The name is the distractor; the device is the answer.

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: According to the lecturer, why was John Harrison's chronometer so significant?
options: It allowed sailors to establish their longitude while at sea
It was the first clock cheap enough for ordinary sailors to own
It enabled ships to calculate their latitude for the first time
questions.explanation: "Establishing longitude required knowing the exact time back at their home port." Latitude is mentioned in the sentence immediately before, which is exactly why it is offered as an option.

questions.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write NO MORE THAN ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.sentence: In the nineteenth century, the growth of the ___ forced towns to abandon their separate local times.
questions.explanation: "It was the expansion of the railways that made this intolerable." The plural is used in the recording, so write it that way.

questions.sentence: Today's most precise clocks count the extremely rapid oscillations of ___ atoms.
questions.explanation: "Modern atomic clocks work by counting the natural oscillations of caesium atoms."

questions.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

questions.question: Why does satellite navigation depend on extremely accurate timekeeping?
options: Satellites must be launched at exactly the right moment
A tiny timing error would produce a large error in position
Atomic clocks are too heavy to be carried on most satellites
questions.explanation: "An error of a millionth of a second would put your position out by hundreds of metres." The answer is a cause-and-effect relationship, not a single word to catch.
